lead: An ion-sensitive field-effect transistor, or ISFET, is a MOSFET with no metal gate. The sample and an ion-selective membrane sit where the gate was, and bound ions change the surface charge. That change shifts the threshold voltage, so a chemical concentration appears as an electrical signal. ISFETs measure pH in small volumes; enzyme-coated EnFETs measure penicillin, glucose or urea; antibody-coated IMFETs detect antigens without a label. They are used in portable meters, lab-on-chip systems and implantable chemical sensing.
prereq: You need: 4.3 for potentiometric transduction, and the MOSFET ideas of gate, threshold voltage and subthreshold swing from basic electronics.

blocks.text: An ISFET is a MOSFET (metal-oxide-semiconductor field-effect transistor) with the metal gate removed. Source and drain are n⁺ (heavily doped n-type) regions in p-silicon, with a channel between them. The gate stack is a thin silicon dioxide layer plus silicon nitride (Si₃N₄) or tantalum oxide (Ta₂O₅), exposed to the sample electrolyte. A reference electrode, usually Ag/AgCl, sits in the sample and completes the circuit. For ion selectivity, an ion-selective membrane covers the gate. The threshold voltage V<sub>T</sub> is the gate voltage at which the channel just forms; drain current I<sub>D</sub> flows from drain to source when V<sub>T</sub> is exceeded.

Ions bind to surface sites such as SiOH or TaOH. The bound charge changes the surface potential. The surface potential adds in series with the applied gate voltage, and the electrolyte double-layer capacitance divides with the gate capacitance, so only part of the surface potential appears across the channel and shifts V<sub>T</sub>. At fixed gate voltage, I<sub>D</sub> changes. The site-binding model describes the surface charge against pH; only its name is needed here. The device is small, fast and batch-fabricated, and its low output impedance suits electrical readout.

sections.h3: pH ISFET, EnFET and the Nernst slope

blocks.text: At 25 °C the pH response follows the Nernst slope: 59.16 mV per pH unit. Run the ISFET at constant drain current with a feedback gate. The feedback adjusts the gate voltage V<sub>G</sub> to hold I<sub>D</sub> fixed. V<sub>G</sub> then follows the surface potential, so the ISFET becomes a pH meter with an electrical output. If the gate voltage is held fixed instead, the drain current changes; in the subthreshold region the change is set by the subthreshold swing, typically 60–80 mV per decade of current. Temperature must be known because the Nernst slope is proportional to absolute temperature.

blocks.where: ΔV<sub>G</sub> is the gate-voltage shift; ΔpH is the pH change; R is 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹; T is absolute temperature in K; F is 96485 C mol⁻¹; the sign is set by surface charge and feedback polarity.

blocks.text: An enzyme field-effect transistor (EnFET) is the same device with an enzyme layer over the gate. The enzyme reaction changes local pH or charge. Penicillinase on penicillin produces penicilloic acid; glucose oxidase on glucose produces gluconic acid; urease on urea produces ammonia and raises pH. The enzyme layer sets selectivity, and its kinetics set range and detection limit (see 4.2 and 4.5).

An immunologically sensitive field-effect transistor (IMFET) is an ISFET with an antibody immobilised on the gate or in a membrane over it. Antigen binding adds charge near the surface. If that charge lies within the Debye length, it changes the surface potential and shifts V<sub>T</sub>. Detection is label-free: no fluorescent or radioactive tag is needed. The Debye length is the distance over which counterions screen charge; it is about 1 nm in physiological salt, so charge farther away is screened. Undiluted serum therefore gives a weak direct signal; dilute the sample or use a membrane that brings binding close to the surface. A neutral antigen gives little direct charge signal; a charged sandwich label can help but is no longer strictly label-free.

Readout uses a constant-current or constant-voltage circuit. A differential pair has one sensing ISFET and one reference ISFET without antibody, or with inactive antibody. Subtraction removes common drift, temperature and light effects. CMOS (complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor) integration puts many ISFETs and amplifiers on one chip for multi-ion or multi-antibody arrays.

items: Oxidation grows a thick field oxide on p-silicon.
Photolithography and etching open the source and drain windows.
Diffusion or ion implantation forms the n⁺ source and drain; annealing follows.
A second lithography step opens the gate region, and a thin gate oxide (SiO₂) is grown there.
The sensing layer, Si₃N₄ by LPCVD or Ta₂O₅, is deposited over the gate oxide.
Contact holes are opened and aluminium or gold is deposited for the source and drain contacts.
Encapsulation with epoxy, polyimide or silicon nitride covers everything except the gate window; an ion-selective or enzyme membrane is added last.

blocks.text: Practical limits are drift, hysteresis, light sensitivity and reference-electrode instability. Drift is a slow change in V<sub>T</sub> from hydration or ion migration. Hysteresis makes the reading depend on the previous pH. Light creates carriers in silicon and shifts the current. The reference electrode's drift adds directly to V<sub>G</sub>, so it must be stable. Temperature control matters because the Nernst slope changes with T. The gate window is the only place where the gate insulator touches the sample; everything else is sealed by epoxy, polyimide or nitride.

figure.caption: An ISFET is a MOSFET whose metal gate is replaced by the sample: the SiO₂ gate oxide carries a Si₃N₄ or Ta₂O₅ sensing layer, and the Ag/AgCl reference electrode sits in the sample above it. With feedback holding I<sub>D</sub> fixed, a pH fall from 7.4 to 7.1 moves V<sub>G</sub> by 17.7 mV.

examples.question: A pH ISFET has a Nernst slope of 59.16 mV per pH unit at 25 °C and a subthreshold swing of 70 mV per decade. The sample pH falls from 7.4 to 7.1. (a) Find the gate-voltage shift at constant drain current with a feedback gate. (b) Find the drain-current ratio at constant gate voltage. (c) Explain why an IMFET signal from one electronic charge per bound antigen needs a differential pair and averaging.
steps: |ΔV<sub>G</sub>| = 59.16 mV/pH × 0.3 pH = 17.748 mV ≈ 17.7 mV. pH falling raises the surface potential, so the feedback gate moves down by 17.7 mV to hold I<sub>D</sub>.
At constant V<sub>G</sub>, use S = 70 mV/decade: I<sub>D</sub> ratio = 10<sup>|ΔV|/S</sup> = 10<sup>17.7/70</sup> = 10<sup>0.253</sup> = 1.79.
So I<sub>D</sub> rises by about 1.8 times at fixed V<sub>G</sub>; the sign follows the surface-charge direction.

For (c), q = 1.602 × 10<sup>−19</sup> C and ΔV = q/C. A 10 µm × 10 µm gate with 10 nm of SiO₂ (relative permittivity 3.9) has C = 8.854 × 10<sup>−12</sup> × 3.9 × 10<sup>−10</sup> / 10<sup>−8</sup> = 0.35 pF, so ΔV ≈ 1.602 × 10<sup>−19</sup> / 3.5 × 10<sup>−13</sup> = 0.46 µV. A smaller gate has a smaller C and a larger shift, up to a few millivolts for nanoscale devices. One charge on a normal gate is far below drift and noise; a reference ISFET subtracts common drift, and averaging many bound antigens and many readings reduces random noise.
examples.answer: The constant-current gate-voltage shift is 17.7 mV downward, the constant-voltage drain current rises by a factor of about 1.79, and one bound charge shifts a 10 µm gate by only about 0.5 µV.

examples.question: The same pH ISFET measures blood at 37 °C, but its read-out still assumes the 25 °C slope. The pH falls from 7.40 to 7.10. Find the true slope, the gate shift, and the pH change the uncorrected meter reports.
steps: The meter divides by the 25 °C slope: 18.46 / 59.16 = 0.312 pH.
Error = 0.312 − 0.300 = 0.012 pH, about 4 % of the change.
examples.answer: The gate moves 18.5 mV and the uncorrected meter reports a fall of 0.312 pH instead of 0.300; a temperature sensor on the chip removes this error.

traps: Sign slip: at constant current the feedback gate moves to compensate; do not say the drain current changes by 59 mV/pH.
Mixing readouts: the Nernst slope applies to gate voltage at constant current; the subthreshold swing applies to current at constant gate voltage.
Ignoring Debye screening in IMFET: undiluted serum screens charge beyond about 1 nm; binding must be close to the surface.
Treating ISFET as a glass electrode: it has no glass bulb and needs a stable reference electrode; reference drift adds to V<sub>G</sub>.
Forgetting drift, hysteresis, light and temperature: all shift V<sub>T</sub> or the slope; a single calibration point is not enough.

quiz.q: Which layers replace the MOSFET metal gate in an ISFET?
quiz.a: The sample electrolyte and an ion-selective membrane over a gate oxide or nitride; a reference electrode completes the circuit.

quiz.q: Why does an IMFET need antigen binding within about 1 nm of the gate?
quiz.a: At physiological salt, counterions screen charge beyond the Debye length (~1 nm); farther charge does not shift the surface potential enough.

quiz.q: An ISFET has 59.16 mV/pH at 25 °C. pH changes by 0.5. Find the constant-current gate shift.
Why use a differential pair with a reference ISFET?
quiz.a: It subtracts common drift, temperature and light effects; the sensing signal is small.

quiz.q: Name two gate insulators used in ISFETs.
quiz.a: Si₃N₄ and Ta₂O₅; SiO₂ is also used.
Constant current: feedback gate voltage follows the Nernst slope. Constant voltage: drain current changes by the subthreshold swing.

quiz.q: S = 60 mV/decade and gate shift is 30 mV. Find the current ratio.
Why is undiluted serum hard for an IMFET?
quiz.a: High ionic strength gives Debye length ~1 nm, so antigen charge is screened; dilution or a membrane is needed, and nonspecific binding adds error.

beyond: Not for the exam. CMOS ISFET arrays place thousands of pH-sensitive pixels on one chip for point-of-care and semiconductor sequencing. Research explores nanoribbon and graphene ISFETs, reference-less differential cells and antifouling membranes. Search for the site-binding model, Debye-length screening and CMOS ISFET arrays.
